stories.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth while a computer problem pauses its science data
paragraphs: NASA says Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers), at 2:16 a.m. PST on Nov. 18, 2026, after more than 49 years of travel. NASA says the team at its Jet Propulsion Laboratory heard from the probe 24 hours later, early Thursday, Nov. 19, the time its radio transmission needed to reach Earth at the speed of light. No human-made object had reached that distance before, Live Science notes.

The milestone came during a fault. According to NASA, the team has not received science or engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14. The spacecraft is still sending its carrier wave, the radio tone that normally carries that data, and engineers used it together with trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day mark. NASA says they continue to analyze the problem.

Live Science reports that, according to NASA, the problem likely stems from the onboard computer that collects data from the science instruments and packages it for Earth. A similar problem in November 2023 stopped Voyager 1's science data until engineers fixed it in June 2024, and the team is approaching the new fault the same way. "We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," project manager Suzanne Dodd said at a NASA news conference on Nov. 19, adding that she is confident the data will flow again. She also said it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft.

ScienceDaily, publishing NASA material, says both Voyagers lose about four watts of power each year, and that earlier in 2026 engineers switched off three devices on Voyager 1 and replaced them with lower-power alternatives. Those steps are expected to keep the current instruments running until at least summer 2027, the 50th anniversary of the launches. Live Science says Voyager 1 has two science instruments still working, a magnetometer and a plasma wave detector, and that Voyager 2 is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035.

image.alt: Artist's concept of NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft in interstellar space

stories.title: Astronomers watch two stars merge in the Andromeda galaxy from start to finish for the first time
paragraphs: Astronomers have for the first time followed two stars, a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the Sun, through a complete merger, Live Science reports. The event, catalogued as AT 2025abao and nicknamed "Bao," happened in the Andromeda galaxy, the closest major galaxy to ours. The study, led by Columbia University astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar, was published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

According to Universe Today, the system brightened slowly in visible light from 2018 to early 2025, then faded in visible light while growing brighter in infrared. In October 2025 it erupted, brightening 100 times over 25 days. The James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the eruption peaked, which Karambelkar called the earliest follow-up ever of an event like this. Live Science says the changes were first picked up by NASA's now-retired NEOWISE spacecraft, with follow-up from an infrared instrument at Palomar Observatory.

The researchers describe a process called common envelope evolution, in which two stars end up orbiting inside a shared cloud of gas that drags them together. Simulations matched to the Webb data indicate the larger star was about seven times the Sun's mass, 350 times its radius and 18,000 times brighter, while the companion had about 0.7 solar masses, Universe Today reports. The pair merged after about seven orbits, roughly seven years.

Live Science reports that instead of exploding as a supernova or collapsing into a neutron star or black hole, the merged system appears to have settled into a single massive star. Universe Today notes that only a few dozen similar eruptions, called luminous red novae, have been detected so far, and that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's survey is expected to find hundreds, possibly thousands.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); image processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI), via Universe Today
image.alt: Telescope views of the stellar merger AT 2025abao in the Andromeda galaxy, before, during and after its eruption

stories.title: This year's El Niño has broken ocean temperature records, and California is preparing for its peak
paragraphs: Science News reports that by Oct. 18, the ocean area researchers use to measure El Niño's strength averaged more than 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit) for the first time on record, and kept rising. In September, the region's daily average sea surface temperature reached more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average, the most extreme level ever recorded. The World Meteorological Organization predicts temperatures there may peak at 3.7 degrees above average by January, according to Science News. The two previous strongest El Niños on record began in 1997 and 2015.

According to Science News, the warm water fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record, with 331 units of accumulated cyclone energy by mid-October, beating the 2018 record of 318, while the Atlantic season was extraordinarily quiet. The magazine says rain and drought effects are expected around the world through spring 2027, and that the event's heat could combine with human-caused warming to make 2027 the hottest year on record.

In a second article, Science News reports that California officials are going door to door to warn residents, and the state has stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators and cleared storm drains. Giant waves have already hit the coast, and the peak is expected by late November or early December, lasting through February or March. A preprint posted Sept. 30 on EarthArXiv suggests the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher than in earlier El Niño years along coastlines from Alaska to Chile.

For comparison, Science News says the 1997-98 El Niño, the strongest before this one, was linked to more than 22,000 deaths worldwide, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

image.credit: ERA5, Climate Pulse/C3S/ECMWF, via Science News
image.alt: Map of Pacific Ocean surface temperatures on Nov. 14, 2026, showing El Niño's band of warm water off South America

stories.title: NASA pauses science on the Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter while teams work separate hardware problems
paragraphs: NASA said on Nov. 19 that teams for its Perseverance Mars rover and its 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter are investigating separate technical issues, and that science work on both missions is temporarily paused. According to NASA, the rover is stable and communicating with the team, and both missions are hoped to return to science by the end of November.

On Oct. 30, NASA says, Perseverance's primary downlink radio failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the rover's main computer, which triggered onboard fault protection: the rover switched to its backup UHF radio and entered safe mode. "In this case, there were 25 missed heartbeats, or about 100 seconds of silence," NASA wrote, quoting project manager Steven Lee of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. After recovery, engineers found the backup radio was transmitting at about half its expected power, and the team stopped using both radios. The rover is now talking directly to NASA's Deep Space Network over its high-gain antenna at a much lower data rate, so instrument work and new raw images are on hold; Space.com notes the mission website had posted no new raw images since Nov. 7.

Odyssey was in safe mode from Nov. 4 to 6, and engineers then determined that one of its reaction wheels, which help orient the spacecraft, had stopped spinning, according to NASA. The orbiter has four wheels, one of which failed in 2013, and needs at least three. NASA says that without them Odyssey would have to rely on its hydrazine thrusters, and the team estimates it has only enough fuel to do that for one to two months. In one test the faulty wheel moved when commanded, and further tests are under way to see whether it can be recovered.

NASA notes that Odyssey, which entered Mars orbit in October 2001 on a mission planned for just over 2.5 years, has operated around Mars longer than any other mission and made the first global maps of the composition of the Martian surface. Space.com adds that Perseverance had just set a new off-Earth driving record on Oct. 11, passing the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark held by NASA's Opportunity rover.

image.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech (Viking Orbiter 1 mosaic), via NASA Science
image.alt: Mosaic of Mars made from images captured by NASA's Viking Orbiter 1
